articles.title: New Simulations Connect the First Galaxies to the Universe We See Today
articles.description: In a recent study, researchers at the international MEGATRON project used some of the most detailed simulations of the early Universe to investigate how the first stars and galaxies formed.
articles.summary: Advanced MEGATRON simulations connect the first galaxies formed after the Big Bang to the modern universe we observe today. This breakthrough reveals how early cosmic structures evolved into present-day galaxies.

articles.title: NASA’s Webb finds signs of Mars-sized worlds smashing together
articles.description: NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope is giving astronomers a glimpse of the kinds of violent collisions that may have shaped our own solar system, including the giant impact thought to have created the Moon. By studying 21 rare “extreme debris disks” around young stars, researchers found that their dust can reveal the scale and intensity of planetary collisions.
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope detected evidence of Mars-sized planetary collisions, revealing how violent cosmic impacts shaped planetary systems. This discovery deepens our understanding of planet formation processes across the universe.

articles.title: Nobel physics prize awarded for discovery of ‘ghostly messengers’ from the cosmos
articles.description: Belgium-born Francis Halzen has won for the detection of high energy neutrino particle from space.
articles.summary: Belgium-born physicist Francis Halzen won the Nobel Prize in Physics for detecting high-energy neutrinos from space, revealing ghostly cosmic messengers. This recognition honors groundbreaking work that opened a new window on the universe.

articles.title: What are 'ghost particles' that pass through your body every second? Francis Halzen wins Physics Nobel for catching them in South Pole ice
articles.description: Francis Halzen has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for his groundbreaking work on the IceCube Neutrino Observatory. This observatory detects high-energy neutrinos originating from extreme cosmic events beyond our Solar System. The project has pro…
articles.summary: Francis Halzen received the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for capturing high-energy neutrinos in South Pole ice through the IceCube Neutrino Observatory. This achievement revolutionizes how scientists observe the cosmos through ghost particles.

articles.title: Francis Halzen wins Nobel Prize in physics for work on high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin
articles.description: Francis Halzen won the Nobel Prize in physics on Tuesday for his contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and his discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin.
articles.summary: Francis Halzen won the Nobel Prize in Physics for his contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and discoveries of astrophysical high-energy neutrinos. This landmark award celebrates transformative advances in particle astrophysics.

articles.title: 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics awarded to Francis Halzen for discovery of high-energy neutrinos
articles.description: Francis Halzen is a leader in the study of neutrinos, ghostly particles from across the universe that hint at exciting new physics
articles.summary: Francis Halzen earned the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering high-energy neutrinos from across the universe, revealing cosmic secrets. His work on these ghostly particles hints at exciting new physics beyond current understanding.

articles.title: Daily briefing: Physics Nobel for founder of neutrino-hunting observatory
articles.description: Francis Halzen has won the Nobel Prize in Physics for his work in founding the IceCube Neutrino Observatory. Plus, a call to prevent a privacy crisis driven by smart glasses and has flu season come early?
articles.summary: Francis Halzen wins the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for founding the IceCube Neutrino Observatory. A major recognition of groundbreaking work in high-energy neutrino detection.

articles.title: Nobel physics prize awarded for detection of ghostly neutrinos
articles.description: Francis Halzen wins the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on a pioneering high-energy neutrino observatory at the South Pole.
articles.summary: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics awarded for the detection of ghostly neutrinos through a pioneering high-energy observatory. A landmark achievement in astrophysics.

articles.description: A visualization of a dark Moon eclipsing the Sun is marked with handwritten notes in this April 6, 2026, screenshot from an Artemis II crew member’s tablet. NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman (in blue) and Victor “Ike” Glover (in green) and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) Jeremy Hansen (in red) observed impact flashes and their locations, which […]
articles.summary: NASA's Artemis II mission captures stunning visualization of a lunar eclipse with annotated Moon and Sun imagery from April 2026.

articles.title: Astronomers Solve Cosmic Cold Case with NASA Hubble Data
articles.description: Diligent sleuthing by astronomers uncovered a surprising chemical clue that indicates the white dwarf star HS 0209+0832 may host a second-generation planet. This artist’s concept released on Oct. 5, 2026, depicts that possible explanation. The white dwarf is the “dead” core of a star that burned through all of its nuclear fuel and lost its outer […]
articles.summary: Astronomers solve a cosmic mystery using NASA Hubble data, discovering surprising chemical evidence about white dwarf star HS 0209+0832.

articles.title: Science begins for Smile
articles.description: On 23 September, the European-Chinese Smile mission was declared ready to start revealing how Earth responds to the wind of charged particles from the Sun. This follows a busy in-space commissioning period since the spacecraft launched on 19 May and reached its target orbit for science operations on 20 June.
articles.summary: The European-Chinese Smile mission begins science operations, investigating Earth's dynamic response to solar wind interactions.

articles.title: Galaxies in a cosmic house of mirrors
articles.description:
Image:
			
This NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope Picture of the Month features galaxies in great detail that have been warped and multiplied like they’ve stepped into a house of mirrors. The brilliant golden galaxies splashed across this image belong to a galaxy cluster called MACS J0454.1-0300. The orange galaxies concentrated on one side of the cluster are not actually part of the cluster and are much farther away from us.
MACS J0454.1-0300 is itself immensely distant: the light from these galaxies has been travelling to us for so long that we’re seeing the cluster as it was when the Universe was about 8 billion years old. While this galaxy cluster is a valuable scientific target in its own right, the real stars of this image are the galaxies that appear warped and stretched, like a painting that has been smeared by a giant hand.
The way these galaxies look is the result of gravitational lensing, in which the enormous mass of a foreground object such as a galaxy cluster bends and magnifies the light from a more distant object in the background. Gravitational lensing allows astronomers to observe galaxies, star clusters and even individual stars that are too far away for our telescopes to see under normal conditions. While the large, orange galaxies appear obviously distorted, look carefully at some of the small reddish background galaxies throughout this picture: even at the very edges of the frame, there are galaxies whose images have been bent into tiny arcs by MACS J0454.1-0300’s gravity.
The gravitationally lensed areas show multiple images of galaxies from when the Universe was young: a group of galaxies 2 billion years after the Big Bang, and a single galaxy just 800 million years old after the Big Bang. The galaxy group appears to be going through a merger, resulting in an enormous burst of star formation.
Astronomers have also identified individual bright ‘knots’ within the gravitationally lensed areas, corresponding to regions as small as 5 light-years across. These tiny clumps appear magnified by a factor of more than 300, in some cases.
A NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope image of this same cluster was released in 2014. Take a moment to compare the two images; the difference between them is dramatic. The new Webb image reveals hundreds of galaxies missing from the earlier image. These galaxies were there all along, but Webb is much more sensitive to their much redder light.
The data behind this image come from two observing programmes (#5058, PI: Furtak; #6882, PI: Fujimoto) that leverage the ability of massive galaxy clusters to bring distant objects into view.
[Image Description: A massive galaxy cluster, made of many golden elliptical galaxies with the largest, brightest one in the centre. Heavily distorted orange galaxies appear all around the cluster, the largest concentrated in a large arc around the cluster's centre; these are images of very distant galaxies, created by gravitational lensing. A few galaxies are large and bluish-white in colour; bright, nearby stars are the same colour.]
Release on esawebb.org
articles.summary: James Webb Space Telescope reveals intricate details of distant galaxies through gravitational lensing in a cosmic mirror effect.

articles.title: Successful Earth flyby improves Juice’s course to Jupiter
articles.description: The European Space Agency’s Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer (Juice) skimmed the very outer edge of Earth’s atmosphere on 28 September, using the gravity of our home planet to alter its route to Jupiter using very little fuel.
articles.summary: ESA's Juice spacecraft successfully performs Earth gravity assist maneuver, optimizing its trajectory toward Jupiter's icy moons.

articles.title: A galaxy spinning out of sync
articles.description:
Image:
			
Though the spiral galaxy in this new image by the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope seems serene, it hides a chaotic secret. This galaxy is NGC 4698, and it lies about 55 million light-years away in the constellation Virgo. It’s one of over one thousand galaxies in the Virgo Cluster, the nearest large cluster of galaxies bound together by gravity.
As a spiral galaxy similar to our own Milky Way galaxy, NGC 4698 has spiral arms that curl around within a thin disc of stars, gas and dust. Its centre is dominated by a galactic bulge.
The diffuse off-white glow of the galaxy’s bulge comes from stars smaller, older, and cooler than the massive blue stars that dot the galaxy’s outer disc. These tightly packed stars orbit a supermassive black hole containing millions of times the Sun’s mass. Scientists have found signs that this black hole is actively growing, drawing gas inward with its gravitational pull.
With a flat, starry disc and diffusely glowing centre, NGC 4698 looks a lot like a typical spiral galaxy — but this galaxy is far from normal. NGC 4698 is one of only a few known spiral galaxies with a bulge that extends out from the disc at a right angle. The elongation is faintly visible in this Hubble image, which shows the ghostly glow of the starry bulge peeking above and below the dusty disc. What’s more, the stars and gas nearest the galaxy’s centre rotate perpendicular to the rest of the disc.
What could cause a galaxy to be so out of sync? Astronomers have found that the culprit likely lies outside the galaxy. If NGC 4698 funneled in gas from an outside source, the newly collected gas could have formed a disc of gas and stars in the galaxy’s centre, at an angle relative to the rest of the disc. Some observations suggest that this galaxy once experienced a minor galactic merger, as evidenced by a short ‘tail’ of hydrogen streaming from one side of the galaxy.
The data used to create this image come from an observing programme (#18103; PI: Thilker) focusing on galaxies in the Virgo Cluster.
[Image Description: A spiral galaxy viewed at an angle, with a bright central bulge and winding spiral arms. The arms form a ring around the galaxy, without appearing to reach its centre. Prominent red-brown dust lanes weave through the arms, which are also dotted with bright blue and reddish regions of star formation. The galaxy is set against a dark background scattered with stars and faint distant galaxies.]
Release on esawebb.org
articles.summary: The Hubble Space Telescope reveals a spiral galaxy with surprising dynamics that challenge our understanding of galactic rotation. This discovery provides insights into complex gravitational interactions within galaxy systems.

articles.title: Thousands of Black Holes Could Be Lurking in Our Backyard—and You Can Help Find Them
articles.description: According to stellar evolution models, there should be hundreds of millions of black holes floating around in our galaxy. But so far we’ve only found 70. That’s in large part because they are so hard to find, but a citizen science project from the University of Southampton is actively seeking out these hidden monsters with the help of tens of thousands of amateur astronomers through a project on Zooniverse called [Black Hole Hunters](https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/cobalt-lensing/black-hole-hunters).
articles.summary: Hundreds of millions of wandering black holes may exist throughout our galaxy, and citizen scientists can help discover them. This research opens new avenues for understanding black hole populations and their role in galactic evolution.

articles.title: Wandering Black Holes May Hold Clues to the Evolution of the Universe
articles.description: According to new research, "wandering" black holes may have left an imprint on the Universe as they traveled for billions of years.
articles.summary: Traveling black holes may have shaped the evolution of the universe as they journeyed through space over billions of years. This research reveals how black holes influence cosmic structure and development.

articles.title: Galaxy Evolution Can be Affected by Black Hole Jets
articles.description: In recent decades, astronomers have found evidence that supermassive black holes can really mess with their galaxies' evolution. They gobble up material intended for star formation, quenching the birth of stars. Conversely, jets streaming away from those hungry monsters can also energize gas-rich regions and enhance the chances of a galaxy birthing batches of stars in those areas.
articles.summary: Jets from supermassive black holes significantly influence galaxy evolution and structure throughout the cosmos. This discovery demonstrates the profound impact black holes have on their galactic environments.

articles.title: A Buried Volcano on the Moon Hints At An Ancient Lunar Dynamo
articles.description: Scientists know for certain the moon doesn’t currently have a magnetosphere. But they’ve been debating for decades about whether it ever did. Data from both Apollo samples and orbital scientific instruments have proven divisive, and so the debate still rages. But a new paper from researchers at ETH Zurich, DLR, and the Institute of Applied Geosciences hopes to resolve the debate once and for all - by definitively proving that the Moon did, indeed, once have a magnetic dynamo.
articles.summary: A buried volcanic structure on the Moon provides evidence of an ancient magnetic field, suggesting the Moon once had a dynamic core. This discovery reshapes our understanding of lunar geology and history.

articles.title: Chandra X-ray Observatory Drops New View of our Galaxy’s Unruly Centre
articles.description: The core of the Milky Way is a dense, active, messy region, dominated by a supermassive black hole called Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*) hiding at the heart of the galaxy. But Sgr A* is only a supporting actor in this stunning new image from the Chandra X-ray Observatory.
articles.summary: The Chandra X-ray Observatory reveals dynamic activity at the Milky Way's center around the supermassive black hole Sagittarius A*. This imagery showcases the energetic phenomena surrounding our galaxy's core.

articles.title: Neutrons, Rotating Black Holes, and a Galactic PeVatron at the Center of the Milky Way
articles.description: Supermassive black holes generate tremendous amounts of energy through their accretion disks and jets. But they can also generate energy through the magnetic Penrose process. A new study looks at how we might observe this process through multimessenger astronomy.
articles.summary: Research explores how rotating black holes and neutron stars generate extraordinary energy through accretion and jets, with evidence of a galactic particle accelerator at the Milky Way's center. This study illuminates extreme physics in the most violent cosmic environments.

articles.title: Alcohol in space: Exotic methanol discovered in planet-building zones
articles.description: An international team of astronomers using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), of which the U.S. National Science Foundation National Radio Astronomy Observatory is a partner (NSF NRAO), has combined expertise from across the globe to open a new window on how the organic molecules that seed planets, and potentially life, form in space.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: The ALMA observatory has detected exotic methanol in planet-forming regions around stars, revealing unexpected chemistry in protoplanetary disks. This finding provides insights into how planetary systems form and evolve.

articles.title: Simulated moon soil and recyclable thermoplastics could help build future space infrastructure
articles.description: Transporting material from Earth to the moon is an expensive proposition: By some estimates, moving a single kilogram (2.2 pounds) can cost more than $1 million. Any plan to build a permanent human habitat up there will depend on bringing that sky-high cost down.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Researchers develop methods to build lunar infrastructure using simulated moon soil and recyclable thermoplastics, reducing costly Earth-to-Moon transportation. This innovation promises to enable sustainable expansion of human presence on the Moon.

articles.title: Webb captures commotion from nebula's stellar jets
articles.description: The NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope has unveiled numerous stars formerly hidden by clouds of dust in a stellar nursery known as NGC 7129—a cauldron of cosmic creation, 3,300 light-years from Earth. Webb captured infrared light, which pierces through the dense matter that scatters or absorbs other types of light. This region, rife with stellar objects in different stages of their lives, offers an opportunity to explore how stars shape their surroundings.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope reveals hidden stars in a stellar nebula using its powerful infrared capabilities to penetrate cosmic dust. This observation demonstrates how stellar jets shape star-forming regions and unveil previously invisible stellar populations.

articles.title: A gamma-ray burst's engine stayed active for nearly a month, breaking the previous record
articles.description: Astronomers have observed the longest-lasting central engine activity ever recorded from a gamma-ray burst. The burst occurred at a redshift of 0.8577, and the activity lasted about 27 days in the burst's own rest frame—around 20 days longer than the previous record. The paper, posted to the arXiv preprint server on Sept. 18, explores different mechanisms that could be powering this puzzling burst.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Astronomers observed the longest-lasting gamma-ray burst engine activity ever recorded, breaking previous records by remaining active for nearly a month. This discovery provides new insights into the extreme physics governing these cosmic explosions.

articles.title: Webb finds a surprising atmosphere on a scorching lava world
articles.description: The James Webb Space Telescope has found strong evidence that the rocky lava world HD 3167 b has an atmosphere, despite circling its star every 24 hours under extreme heat. The surprising discovery could help scientists understand how rocky planets retain atmospheres and what the young, molten Earth may once have looked like.
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope found compelling evidence of an atmosphere on the scorching lava world HD 3167 b, defying expectations. This surprising discovery challenges existing models of atmospheric retention on extreme exoplanets.

articles.title: Physicists just saw quarks make waves in the Big Bang’s primordial soup
articles.description: Physicists at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider have captured the clearest evidence yet that quark-gluon plasma, the scorching-hot matter that filled the newborn universe, behaves like a true liquid. By tracking individual quarks as they blasted through the plasma, researchers saw them leave behind ripples, splashes, and swirling wakes much like a duck moving through water. The finding suggests this primordial “soup” is so dense that it can slow speeding quarks and respond collectively as a fluid.
articles.summary: Physicists at CERN's Large Hadron Collider captured the clearest evidence yet of quark-gluon plasma waves, the primordial matter from the Big Bang. This breakthrough provides unprecedented insights into the universe's earliest moments.

articles.title: Scientists find a surprising clue to why the universe’s expansion doesn’t add up
articles.description: Tiny magnetic fields created shortly after the Big Bang may help explain the long-running disagreement over how fast the universe is expanding. Detailed simulations show that these primordial fields could have changed the formation of hydrogen in the early universe, affecting the cosmic microwave background and the expansion rate inferred from it.
articles.summary: Tiny magnetic fields created shortly after the Big Bang may help resolve the long-standing discrepancy in measurements of the universe's expansion rate. This theoretical advance offers a promising solution to one of cosmology's greatest puzzles.

articles.title: Astronomy’s ‘adrenaline junkies’: Nobel prize captures the thrill of neutrino physics
articles.description: Nature reporter Davide Castelvecchi reflects on covering the fast-moving field of astronomy honoured by the Nobel physics award.
articles.summary: Nobel Prize honors neutrino physics and the pioneering work in this fast-moving field of astronomy. A celebration of scientific discovery and the thrill of breakthrough research.

articles.title: STARMUS FESTIVAL COFOUNDERS SIR BRIAN MAY AND GARIK ISRAELIAN PRESENTED PROFESSOR BRIAN COX WITH THE 2026 STEPHEN HAWKING MEDAL FOR SCIENCE COMMUNICATION
articles.description: LONDON, Oct. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- On October 2nd, At the Royal Astronomical Society in London, Starmus Festival cofounders Sir Brian May and Garik Israelian awarded Professor Brian Cox the prestigious 2026 Stephen Hawking Medal for Science Communication, r…
articles.summary: Professor Brian Cox receives the 2026 Stephen Hawking Medal for Science Communication from Starmus Festival cofounders. Recognition of excellence in inspiring public engagement with science.
